periods.activity_title: Reading the Story of Louis Braille

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 55–57): read-aloud of the informational text on Louis Braille.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the topic by asking students whether they have ever seen raised-dot writing on lift buttons or medicine packaging. Elicit what they know about blindness and how people who cannot see might read.

Let us Read (pp. 55–57): teacher reads the informational text aloud expressively, pausing at key moments — Louis's injury, his arrival at the institute, and his encounter with Night Writing. Students follow along with open textbooks.

Draw students' attention to the Braille alphabet diagram on p. 56. Point out that each letter is made of raised-dot patterns and invite students to trace the dots for two or three letters with a fingertip on the page.

Students re-read the text independently and silently; teacher circulates, prompting with questions such as 'What happened to Louis when he was three?' and 'What is the name of the writing system Louis improved?' to check initial comprehension.

periods.teacher_notes: The new words blacksmith, blind, pincushions, and invented appear in this text; write them on the board and briefly clarify meanings before the read-aloud so students are not halted by unfamiliar vocabulary. Students may confuse Night Writing with Braille — emphasise that Night Writing came first and was too complex, and that Louis simplified it.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion on the Braille Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 58): answer three short-answer questions about the Braille text.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to recall the informational text about Louis Braille by asking a quick oral question: 'Where was Louis taken when he was ten years old?' This draws on the content read together previously and settles the class into the reading spine.

Let us Think A (p. 58): pose the first two questions — 'Describe the Braille alphabet' and 'Why was Night Writing not a success?' — to pairs of students who discuss quietly, then share answers aloud. Teacher guides the class to complete and accurate responses, writing key phrases on the board.

Let us Think A (p. 58): take up the third question — 'What did Louis Braille do to make reading easier for the blind?' — through a whole-class discussion. Highlight the closing line of the text: 'Thus, a blind person taught the world to see,' and ask students what they think it means.
Students write their answers to all three questions in their notebooks individually. Teacher circulates, giving brief verbal feedback on sentence structure and accuracy of content.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often give vague answers to 'Describe the Braille alphabet' — guide them to include both the physical feature (raised dots) and the scope (one symbol for each of the 26 letters). The phrase 'a blind person taught the world to see' is figurative; acknowledge both literal and metaphorical readings if students raise them.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 58): guided discussion on white cane and a world without light.
Let us Speak (p. 58–59): close-eyes touch-and-describe activity with class sharing.

homework.task_brief: Let us Listen (p. 59): listen and repeat the 'spl' cluster words with a family member: spoon, splinter, spin, splash, speak, split, space, splendid.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B (p. 58): raise the two discussion questions — why is the white cane always white, and what difficulties would arise if the world went dark for a day? Students discuss in pairs, then volunteers share their ideas with the class; teacher charts key ideas on the board.

Let us Speak (pp. 58–59): place a collection of small classroom objects (eraser, sharpener, ruler, bottle cap) on a tray. Each student closes their eyes, picks one object, feels it, and then opens their eyes to complete the three sentence frames orally ('The object in my hand was ___ in shape…'). Ask each student to add two more descriptive lines before returning the object.

Let us Listen (p. 59): teacher reads the eight 'spl' cluster words from p. 59 aloud three to four times at a measured pace — spoon, splinter, spin, splash, speak, split, space, splendid — while students listen. Students then repeat as a group, then in rows, then individually as teacher points to volunteers.

Bring the oracy work together by asking: 'What did doing the touch-and-tell activity teach you about how Louis Braille might have experienced the world?' Allow two or three brief responses to close the unit thoughtfully.

periods.teacher_notes: The touch-and-tell activity works best when students genuinely close their eyes rather than peek; circulate quietly and encourage honest engagement. For the listening task, emphasise the difference between 'sp' alone and 'spl' — students at this stage commonly drop the 'l' in the cluster.
materials: Tray with small classroom objects (erasers, sharpeners, bottle caps, etc.)

periods.activity_title: Writing in Braille and Listing Eye Precautions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 60): write Cat, Man, Boy, Jug, and own name using Braille dot patterns (bindis).
Let us Write B (p. 61): list precautions to protect eyes from harm.

time_bands.activity: Let us Write A (p. 60): display the Braille alphabet chart (textbook p. 56) for reference. Model the completed example from p. 60, placing bindis to represent the dot pattern for the first letter of 'Cat.' Explain that each cell of dots stands for one letter and students will do the same for four words plus their own name.

Let us Write A (p. 60): students work independently to represent Cat, Man, Boy, and Jug using the dot-pattern or bindi method, consulting the chart on p. 56 for each letter. Teacher circulates, pointing students back to the chart if a pattern is wrong rather than correcting it directly.

Students write their own names in Braille dot patterns, choosing letters from the chart. Invite one or two volunteers to hold up their name in Braille and let classmates 'decode' it by pointing to the chart.

Let us Write B (p. 61): teacher briefly connects the topic to Louis Braille's accident — sharp tools, fireworks, any sudden injury can harm eyes. Students plan and write a list of at least four precautions to protect eyes from harm; teacher uses think-aloud to model one precaution ('Never play with sharp objects near the face') before students continue independently.

periods.teacher_notes: Bindis or round stickers work well for the dot-pattern writing; if neither is available, students can use a pencil to draw small filled circles following the six-dot cell layout shown on p. 56. For Let us Write B, encourage students to think beyond the fireworks example in the text — spectacles, screen use, and chemical splashes are all valid precautions that show independent thinking.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (pp. 61–62): change six present-continuous sentences to past continuous using was/were + -ing.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn C (pp. 61–62): write the two example sentences from the textbook on the board — one with 'was playing' (Louis Braille) and one with 'were sleeping' (cats). Elicit from students what is happening in each sentence and why one uses 'was' while the other uses 'were.' Establish the rule: singular subject → was + verb-ing; plural subject → were + verb-ing.

Work through the model transformation on the board together: 'I am sleeping' → 'I was sleeping.' Invite a student to identify the subject, a second to check singular or plural, and a third to form the past-continuous version. Do the same with 'The dogs are barking' as a guided step before students continue on their own.

Let us Learn C (pp. 61–62): students complete the remaining four transformations — Grandfather/searching, Sheeba/writing, He/singing, We/playing, The man/using — in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, checking subject-verb agreement and correct -ing formation.
Take up answers orally: call on students to read their transformed sentences aloud. Address any recurring error (e.g., 'we was playing') at the board before closing the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often apply 'was' even with plural subjects ('We was playing') — spend a moment on the 'I/he/she/it → was' versus 'we/they/you → were' distinction before the independent practice. The sentence about Louis Braille from the text ('Louis Braille was playing near his home') makes a strong anchor point because students have just read it in context.

periods.activity_title: Past Continuous in a Picture Story — Tarandeep and the Sparrows

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn D (pp. 62–63): fill six blanks in the Tarandeep picture-story using past-continuous forms from a given word bank.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn D (pp. 62–63): conduct a picture walk through the five-panel story on pp. 62–63. For each panel, ask 'What do you see?' and 'What is the character doing?' — elicit responses in the present continuous to warm up the grammar pattern before students apply it in the past.

Read the paragraph of the Tarandeep story aloud as a class, pausing at each blank. Display the six word-bank options (was clapping, was scattering, were sitting, was hanging, was entering, was feeding) on the board. Model the first blank together: 'She ___ her friends' — ask students which option makes sense with the picture and with the singular subject 'She.'

Students work through the remaining five blanks in their notebooks, checking each option against both the story pictures and the subject of the sentence. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are uncertain: 'Is the subject one person or more than one? Which word — was or were — fits?'

Whole-class answer check: call on students to read one completed sentence each and explain why they chose that option. Correct any mismatches and invite the class to confirm or adjust. Close by asking students to summarise the Tarandeep story in one or two past-continuous sentences of their own.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the singular/plural rule for was/were together in the previous grammar unit, students are ready to apply it in this richer context; the picture panels make subject identification easier and are a useful scaffold for uncertain readers. Watch for students who select an option that is grammatically valid but does not match the picture event — use the images to redirect them rather than simply giving the answer.

periods.activity_title: Feel and Identify — Tactile Exploration and Supporting Classmates

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p. 64): press shapes/letters on paper, close eyes, and identify the raised surface; repeat with a partner.
Let us Explore (p. 64): discuss how classmates can assist children with low vision.

homework.task_brief: Let us Explore (p. 64): find out about the nearest resource centre for people with blindness and note its name and location.

time_bands.activity: Open the unit by asking students to close their eyes and feel the cover of their textbook or a pencil case. Ask: 'What can you tell about this object using only your fingers?' This brief sensory moment directly connects to the Braille principle explored throughout the chapter.

Let us Do (p. 64): each student takes a sheet of paper and, using the back of a pencil or a matchstick, presses a circle, plus sign, or a letter firmly onto the paper. Students then close their eyes, turn the paper over, and run a fingertip along the raised surface to identify their shape. Pairs then exchange papers and try to identify each other's shape by touch alone.

Let us Explore (p. 64): whole-class discussion on supporting classmates with low vision. Teacher poses the question: 'A classmate holds books very close to their eyes or wears thick glasses. What can you do to help them in school?' Students share ideas; teacher lists suggestions on the board (large-print materials, reading aloud, sitting closer to the board, etc.).

Bring the unit together by connecting Louis Braille's invention to the class's own experience: 'You just felt shapes with your fingers — that is exactly how Braille readers experience every word on a page.' Set the homework task from p. 64 and close.

periods.teacher_notes: The pressing activity works best with thinner paper such as a page torn from an exercise book; card stock is too thick to show a clear raised impression. If white clay is available, the same shape-and-feel activity can be done in clay, which gives a more dramatic tactile result.

items.source_lo: Student extracts and extracts key information using an informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Louis Braille's life, his injury, Night Writing, and the Braille alphabet invention.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes why Night Writing was not widely adopted?

options.label: A
options.text: It could only represent numbers, not letters.

options.label: B
options.text: It used ink that faded quickly in the dark.

options.label: C
options.text: It was too complex for ordinary people to learn easily.

options.label: D
options.text: It was used only by sailors and was too wet to handle.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be confusing Night Writing with a maritime signalling system; no such detail appears in the text.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may be thinking of ink-based print rather than the raised-dot nature of Night Writing.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be guessing; the text does not restrict Night Writing to numbers.

items.source_context: Louis Braille's life, his injury, Night Writing, and the Braille alphabet invention.
items.item_stem: The informational text ends with the line: 'Thus, a blind person taught the world to see.' What does this line mean? Write your answer in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Louis Braille was blind himself, yet he created a reading system that helped people with blindness access knowledge and literacy, showing that a person who could not see with his eyes gave the gift of 'seeing' — that is, understanding and learning — to the world.

items.source_context: White cane purpose, imagining darkness, touch-and-describe activity with classroom objects.
items.item_stem: Imagine the world goes completely dark for one full day. Which of the following would be the most immediate difficulty a person might face?

options.label: A
options.text: Feeling bored because there is nothing to do

options.label: D
options.text: Moving safely from one place to another without bumping into things

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student focuses on a practical concern but overlooks the more immediate physical-safety challenge of navigation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student gives a social/emotional answer rather than a physical-safety challenge.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student's answer is about memory rather than the immediate difficulty of functioning without sight.

items.item_stem: Close your eyes. Your teacher will place an object in your hand. Without looking, describe the object to the class using at least three sentences — talk about its shape, size compared to your finger, and what you think it is.

expected_elements: Names a shape (round, flat, rectangular, etc.).
Compares size to finger (longer, shorter, same).
Makes a reasonable guess at the object's identity.

items.visual_stimulus:
Sentence | Correct form
Louis Braille ___ near his home when the accident happened. | was playing / were playing
The children ___ in the classroom when the bell rang. | was sitting / were sitting
She ___ a letter to her friend last night. | was writing / were writing

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. was playing; 2. were sitting; 3. was writing.

Read instructions aloud to them | So they do not miss written information
Share a printout with larger text | So the words are easier to see without straining
Ask if they need help before assuming | So they feel respected and included

items.item_stem: Press a letter or simple shape firmly onto a sheet of thin paper using the back of your pencil. Close your eyes, turn the paper over, and feel the raised surface. Then pass the paper to a partner and ask them to identify the shape by touch alone. Tell the class what shape you made, whether your partner guessed it correctly, and what the activity taught you about reading by touch.

expected_elements: Names the shape or letter pressed onto the paper.
States whether the partner identified it correctly.
Links the experience to how touch-based reading works.
